extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, theoretical physicists, philosophers of mathematics, and advanced students interested in the nature and evaluation of mathematical work
extracted.subtask_description: General criteria and standards for judging mathematical work: its origins, methods, style, and signs of health or degeneration. Emphasizes the dual (empirical and aesthetic) nature of mathematics and how that affects selection, rigour, and valuation of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical origin of mathematical ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Much of the best mathematical inspiration comes from experience and the natural sciences; geometry and calculus originated in empirical problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Von Neumann cites geometry (Euclid, non-Euclidean geometry, general relativity) and calculus (Kepler, Newton, Leibniz, applications in mechanics) as monumental instances where empirical problems or physical insight produced major mathematical advances. He argues that many mathematical concepts have empirical genealogies (sometimes remote), and that re-injection of empirical ideas often rejuvenates subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics' duplicity (empirical and abstract faces)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics has a double nature: it is both closely linked to empirical science and capable of becoming highly abstract and self-contained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One must realize and accept this duplicity; the same mathematician can contribute to both axiomatic/abstract developments and empirically motivated theories (Hilbert's contributions to geometry and to relativity are given as an example). Evaluation should account for both faces rather than insisting on a unitary view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variability and context-dependence of mathematical rigour
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept of mathematical rigour is not immutable; standards of exactness and acceptable proof methods change over time and with philosophical currents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Von Neumann uses the foundations controversy (Cantor, Russell, Brouwer, Weyl, Hilbert, Gödel) to show that what counts as a valid, exact proof has been revised repeatedly. He notes that Gödel’s incompleteness result and the intuitionist/classical debates demonstrate that one cannot take a single notion of 'absolute mathematical rigour' for granted when evaluating work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic variability in proofs and presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in the style and presentation of mathematical proofs affect perceptions of rigour; presentation can fluctuate widely across authors and eras.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Von Neumann observes that presentation differences may be eliminable without new ideas, but sometimes they are so large that they raise doubts about whether authors share the same standards of rigour. He points out historical cases (e.g., eighteenth-/nineteenth-century analysis, Euler vs. Gauss/Jacobi) where significant mathematical results were produced under divergent stylistic and rigour standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic criteria of selection and success
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary criteria for selecting problems and for judging success in mathematics are largely aesthetic: elegance, simplicity, unifying power, architectural structure, and surprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Von Neumann lists specific aesthetic desiderata: simple and elegant classification of many disparate cases, unifying/predicting power, ease in stating the problem, difficulty in approaching it followed by a surprising simplifying twist, and the presence of simple guiding principles underlying lengthy deductions. He compares these criteria to those in creative art and notes their dominance over empirical motives in much of mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of problem selection (lack of externally imposed objectives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians typically have broad freedom to choose problems; importance is often internally (aesthetically) determined rather than imposed by external empirical necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasting with theoretical physics — where problems are often objectively given by experimental anomalies — von Neumann emphasizes that mathematicians may freely move among many subdivisions. Consequently, the mathematician’s criteria for selecting what to work on are more subjective and aesthetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sign of degeneration: excessive abstraction and baroque style
rubrics_metrics.description: When a mathematical field moves far from empirical roots and becomes purely aestheticizing, baroque, and fragmented into many insignificant branches, it is in danger of degeneration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symptoms include proliferation of isolated technicalities and loss of coherent unifying principles. Von Neumann warns that such 'inbreeding' leads to a disorganized mass of details. He prescribes the remedy of re-injecting empirical ideas or engaging with related, more empirically connected subjects to restore vitality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness measured by accessibility to mathematical methods
rubrics_metrics.description: For the natural sciences, a major criterion of success is whether a subject becomes accessible to mathematical (or near-mathematical) methods; scientific progress often follows 'pseudomorphoses' toward mathematical form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Von Neumann traces how biology, chemistry, and physics have successively become amenable to mathematical techniques; he implies that mathematical accessibility/unification is a valuable metric for judging theoretical developments in science, and suggests that mathematics is both a source and receiver of such trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirics can have the final say in otherwise formal disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical or physical considerations may decide among formally equivalent mathematical alternatives when abstract arguments alone are inconclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The discussion of the fifth postulate and non-Euclidean geometry illustrates that despite logical/formal resolutions, empirical input (e.g., general relativity) ultimately influenced acceptance and emphasis. Thus evaluation may properly consider empirical implications or testability where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic acceptance of classical methods despite foundational doubts
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians may accept and use classical (pre-intuitionistic) methods pragmatically if they produce elegant and useful results, even if ultimate philosophical justification is unresolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Von Neumann recounts how, after foundational debates and Gödel’s result, most mathematicians continued to use classical mathematics because it worked and had comparable practical grounding (analogous to accepting the existence of the electron). This suggests a pragmatic criterion: usefulness, elegance, and productivity can justify methods in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration versus plurality as context for impact
rubrics_metrics.description: In theoretical physics impact tends to concentrate on a few core problems; in mathematics impact is distributed across many diverse subdivisions, affecting how one judges significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Von Neumann notes that theoretical physics often focuses communal effort on one or two sharply circumscribed fields, whereas mathematics remains pluralistic. Thus significance in mathematics may be assessed relative to internal aesthetic and disciplinary standards rather than communal concentration on single 'big' problems.
